## Abstract

```{raw} html
<div class="typst article-header"><div class="abstract">The worst-case stabilization time of a self-stabilizing algorithm usually says little about its typical behavior beyond the order of magnitude. This paper revisits the classical self-stabilizing <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>-coloring algorithm with vertices activated at random, one at a time (the random central daemon). Considering the number of color changes as a random variable, we study its mean, variance and, on several families of graphs, its exact distribution. The analysis rests on a reduction: a vertex changes color, at most once, exactly when it is not a local maximum of a uniformly random labeling of the vertices, maxima being taken among the neighbors that share its initial color (the monochrome initial configuration is the slowest case). What can be predicted depends on what is known of the graph. The degree distribution (the view at distance one) gives the mean. The variance needs the view at distance two, in particular the triangles, and the full law needs the whole graph. We give closed-form results, from monochrome and from uniformly random initial configurations, on paths, cycles, random trees, Erdős-Rényi graphs and bipartite random graphs. From a monochrome start, the mean stays within a factor two of the worst case, whereas the variance ranges from zero (disjoint cliques) to order <math><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> (the star on <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> vertices).</div><p class="keywords"><strong>Keywords</strong>: self-stabilization, graph coloring, stabilization time, random daemon, average-case analysis, random permutations, random graphs</p><dl class="meta"><dt>Software</dt><dd><a href="https://github.com/balouf/tinto/tree/v0.1.0">https://github.com/balouf/tinto/tree/v0.1.0</a>, archived at <a href="https://archive.softwareheritage.org/swh:1:rev:79d72a3026ff486616ef0ba83b70e192de339cee;origin=https://github.com/balouf/tinto;visit=swh:1:snp:b56b180e61fa4780760e32a04e9dd7c4fac3fec1"><code>swh:1:rev:79d72a3026ff486616ef0ba83b70e192de339cee</code></a></dd><dt>Acknowledgements</dt><dd>We thank Stephan Wagner for bibliographic references on random trees.</dd></dl></div>
```

{#introduction}
## 1 Introduction

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><p>A self-stabilizing algorithm reaches a legitimate configuration (for a given specification) from any initial one and remains legitimate afterwards <span id="loc-1">[</span><a href="#loc-44" role="doc-biblioref">Alt+19</a>, <a href="#loc-57" role="doc-biblioref">Dij74</a>, <a href="#loc-59" role="doc-biblioref">Dol00</a>]. At each step a <em>daemon</em> chooses which of the enabled processes move. The <em>stabilization time</em> is the number of moves to legitimacy, in the worst case over the initial configuration and the daemon’s choices.</p><p>We consider the classical self-stabilizing <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>-coloring rule on a graph <math><mi>𝐺</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑉</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐸</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> whose vertices are the processes, each holding a color from a palette of at least <math><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> colors, <math><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></math> being the maximum degree <span id="loc-2">[</span><a href="#loc-44" role="doc-biblioref">Alt+19</a>, <a href="#loc-59" role="doc-biblioref">Dol00</a>, <a href="#loc-80" role="doc-biblioref">GT00</a>, <a href="#loc-84" role="doc-biblioref">HJS03</a>]. A process whose color is shared by a neighbor is enabled and, when activated, recolors itself with any color absent from its neighborhood (such a color always exists). Under the central daemon of Dijkstra’s original paper [<a href="#loc-57" role="doc-biblioref">Dij74</a>] (exactly one enabled process per step), the worst case is easy: a recolored process is never in conflict again, so every process moves at most once [<a href="#loc-84" role="doc-biblioref">HJS03</a>]. For any <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math>, the longest execution, over initial configurations and schedules, makes <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> moves, where <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>≔</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝑉</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></math> and <math><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the number of connected components of <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math>. In other words, the worst case sees nothing of <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> beyond <math><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. We wonder what the graph determines once the daemon’s choices are random. Beyond the worst case, self-stabilization mostly studies the expected stabilization time of randomized algorithms, Herman’s token ring being the classic example <span id="loc-3">[</span><a href="#loc-82" role="doc-biblioref">Her90</a>]: the expectation is over their coins, under a synchronous or worst-case daemon. Here, in contrast, we analyze a deterministic algorithm under a random daemon.</p><p>To study typical behavior, we consider the random version of the central daemon that draws the next mover uniformly among the enabled processes. The stabilization time of a deterministic algorithm then becomes a random variable <span id="loc-4">[</span><a href="#loc-62" role="doc-biblioref">DTY15</a>, <a href="#loc-105" role="doc-biblioref">Yam+12</a>]. Observe that the random central daemon is a scheduling abstraction, not a centralized algorithm: each process reads only its neighbors’ colors, and every step is one recoloring by a process in conflict. Counted in recolorings, the stabilization time has the same law when each process is activated by the ticks of its own rate-1 Poisson clock (<a href="#prop-scheduler-free">Proposition 1</a>). Our objective is the law of this random variable: its mean and variance on every graph and from every initial configuration, its full distribution on several families of graphs.</p><p>The key to our approach is as follows: draw a uniformly random ordering of the processes, and let the daemon always serve the enabled process that comes first in it. The execution has the same law as under the random central daemon, and the ordering alone decides which processes move. We call a process a <em>peak</em> when it comes after every neighbor that shares its initial color. A process recolors if and only if it is not a peak, so the stabilization time is exactly <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> minus the number of peaks of a random ordering, whatever free color each move picks.</p><p>From a monochrome start (one common color), the peaks are the local maxima of a random labeling of the graph, an object probability and combinatorics know well: on a path they are the peaks of a random permutation <span id="loc-5">[</span><a href="#loc-55" role="doc-biblioref">DB62</a>, <a href="#loc-63" role="doc-biblioref">Eli16</a>], on a general graph their number is a standard example for Stein’s method <span id="loc-6">[</span><a href="#loc-51" role="doc-biblioref">BRS89</a>], and its expectation is the Caro-Wei bound on the independence number <span id="loc-7">[</span><a href="#loc-53" role="doc-biblioref">Car79</a>, <a href="#loc-103" role="doc-biblioref">Wei81</a>]. We recall the classical results where they are used (<a href="#sec-general">Section 3</a>, <a href="#sec-families">Section 5</a>). To our knowledge, the link between peaks and stabilization time is new, and all our contributions follow from it.</p><p>The mean alone says little: from a monochrome start, on a graph without isolated vertices, it lies between <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></math> and <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, always within a factor two of the worst case (<a href="#prop-mean-extremes">Proposition 3</a>). We therefore study the whole distribution, and the more we know of the graph, the finer the prediction. The mean needs only the degree distribution (<a href="#thm-mean">Theorem 1</a>). The variance needs only, for each pair of processes at distance at most two, the sizes of their common and private neighborhoods, in particular the triangles (<a href="#thm-sfm">Theorem 3</a>, <a href="#eq-var-local">Eq. (6)</a>). The law needs the whole graph. The approach is general: the same proofs cover every graph and every initial configuration, whether monochrome, uniformly random with any number <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> of colors, or fixed, through the subgraph of initially conflicting edges (<a href="#prop-fixed-config">Proposition 2</a>); the monochrome start is the slowest for every ordering of the processes.</p><p>On graphs of bounded degree, the stabilization time is concentrated within order <math><msqrt><mi>𝑛</mi></msqrt></math> of its mean, and is asymptotically normal as soon as its variance grows linearly (<a href="#cor-concentration">Corollary 2</a>). For a monochrome start, the extremes are explicit (<a href="#sec-extremal">Section 4</a>): the variance vanishes exactly on disjoint unions of cliques, never exceeds <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn></math>, and is maximized by the star for every <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math>. Finally, on five families of graphs, we push the analysis to the law itself whenever possible (<a href="#sec-families">Section 5</a>). Besides paths and cycles, these include three random models: uniform random trees, Erdős-Rényi graphs <math><mi>𝐺</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and their bipartite version. Random graphs are a common testbed for simulations in self-stabilization, yet they are rarely analyzed, a recent exception being <span id="loc-8">[</span><a href="#loc-81" role="doc-biblioref">GZ23</a>].</p><p><strong>Related work.</strong> <em>Stabilization time of self-stabilizing coloring.</em> Self-stabilizing vertex coloring was first studied for feasibility on particular graph classes <span id="loc-9">[</span><a href="#loc-78" role="doc-biblioref">GK93</a>, <a href="#loc-100" role="doc-biblioref">SS93</a>], then on arbitrary graphs with explicit stabilization bounds. Gradinariu and Tixeuil [<a href="#loc-80" role="doc-biblioref">GT00</a>] give deterministic <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>-coloring algorithms that stabilize in <math><mi>𝑂</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> moves under an unfair daemon, and a randomized one that stabilizes in <math><mi>𝑂</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0.16666666666666666em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">log</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> expected steps of the distributed daemon, a step possibly moving many processes, the expectation being over the algorithm’s coin flips, against the worst schedule. Hedetniemi, Jacobs and Srimani [<a href="#loc-84" role="doc-biblioref">HJS03</a>] give two algorithms for the central daemon, one reaching a Grundy coloring in a number of moves linear in the number of edges, the other a <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>-coloring in at most <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> moves. Bernard, Devismes, Paroux, Potop-Butucaru and Tixeuil <span id="loc-10">[</span><a href="#loc-47" role="doc-biblioref">Ber+10</a>] analyze a probabilistic coloring algorithm on anonymous networks with one-way links under the unfair distributed daemon. The algorithm’s expected stabilization time, again over its coins and from the worst initial configuration and schedule, goes from <math><mi>𝑂</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> moves with <math><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> colors down to <math><mi>𝑂</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as the palette grows. Other work on the problem is worst-case too: unidirectional coloring <span id="loc-11">[</span><a href="#loc-46" role="doc-biblioref">Ber+09</a>], transformers from local or synchronous to self-stabilizing algorithms <span id="loc-12">[</span><a href="#loc-87" role="doc-biblioref">Joh+24</a>, <a href="#loc-89" role="doc-biblioref">LSW09</a>], dynamic and locally iterative coloring <span id="loc-13">[</span><a href="#loc-45" role="doc-biblioref">BEG22</a>, <a href="#loc-76" role="doc-biblioref">FYZ25</a>]. Two notions of expected stabilization time coexist. In the randomized algorithms above the expectation is over the algorithm’s coins, under a fixed or adversarial daemon <span id="loc-14">[</span><a href="#loc-58" role="doc-biblioref">DIM95</a>], whereas in our work the algorithm is deterministic and the expectation is over a random daemon, possibly also over a random initial configuration or a random graph, so that for a given algorithm it is at most the worst case.</p><p><em>Average-case analyses in self-stabilization.</em> The most studied case is Herman’s randomized token circulation on rings [<a href="#loc-82" role="doc-biblioref">Her90</a>], whose expected stabilization time under synchrony has been bounded with increasing precision <span id="loc-15">[</span><a href="#loc-72" role="doc-biblioref">FMP04</a>, <a href="#loc-77" role="doc-biblioref">FZ15</a>, <a href="#loc-88" role="doc-biblioref">Kie+11</a>, <a href="#loc-94" role="doc-biblioref">Nak05</a>]. Fribourg, Messika and Picaronny <span id="loc-16">[</span><a href="#loc-72" role="doc-biblioref">FMP04</a>, <a href="#loc-73" role="doc-biblioref">FMP06</a>] use coupling to bound two measures of randomized self-stabilizing algorithms: the expected stabilization time and the time after which stabilization has occurred with probability at least <math><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝜀</mi></math>. Both bounds are worst case over the initial configuration, with the probability taken over the algorithm’s coins. Modeling the algorithm as a Markov decision process whose policies are the daemon’s choices, Fribourg and Messika <span id="loc-17">[</span><a href="#loc-71" role="doc-biblioref">FM05</a>] extend these bounds to arbitrary daemons, and Beauquier, Johnen and Messika <span id="loc-18">[</span><a href="#loc-49" role="doc-biblioref">BJM06</a>] reduce the expected stabilization time against the best or the worst daemon to a stochastic shortest-path problem. Exhaustive, symbolic or synthesis-based methods compute such recovery measures on bounded instances <span id="loc-19">[</span><a href="#loc-43" role="doc-biblioref">ABT15</a>, <a href="#loc-67" role="doc-biblioref">Fag+18</a>, <a href="#loc-68" role="doc-biblioref">FB15</a>, <a href="#loc-69" role="doc-biblioref">FBT13</a>, <a href="#loc-102" role="doc-biblioref">Vol+22</a>]. Turau bounds the mean time to repair a single fault for randomized coloring under synchrony <span id="loc-20">[</span><a href="#loc-101" role="doc-biblioref">Tur18</a>]. Instead of solving a Markov chain or decision process, or exploring bounded instances, we reduce the stabilization time to the number of peaks of a random ordering. Speculative stabilization <span id="loc-21">[</span><a href="#loc-56" role="doc-biblioref">DG13</a>] designs algorithms to be fast under a more likely daemon while keeping the worst-case guarantee, whereas here the algorithm is fixed and we measure how long its typical executions take. Closer to ours in spirit, Burman et al. <span id="loc-22">[</span><a href="#loc-52" role="doc-biblioref">Bur+21</a>] analyze leader election in population protocols under the uniform random pairwise scheduler, which is a random daemon, and Giakkoupis and Ziccardi [<a href="#loc-81" role="doc-biblioref">GZ23</a>] give graph-dependent bounds for a synchronous randomized maximal-independent-set process from arbitrary initial states: <math><mi>𝑂</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">log</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> expected rounds on cliques and trees, polylogarithmic rounds with high probability on <math><mi>𝐺</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.</p><p><strong>Organization.</strong> <a href="#sec-model">Section 2</a> fixes the model. <a href="#sec-general">Section 3</a> gives the reduction and the mean and variance theorems, <a href="#sec-extremal">Section 4</a> the extremal results, <a href="#sec-families">Section 5</a> treats the five families, and <a href="#sec-conclusion">Section 6</a> discusses the other daemons and what is left open. The body proves <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a>, <a href="#thm-zero-var">Theorem 4</a>, <a href="#thm-var-upper">Theorem 5</a> and the short corollaries, and sketches the other proofs. The complete proofs, the variance formulas of the <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-colored tree and of the two random-graph families, the Poisson Galton-Watson tree, the figures and the numerical checks are in the appendix, which keeps the section order of the body. The AI-disclosure section follows the references.</p></div>
```

{#sec-model}
## 2 Model

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><p>The rule and the terminology below are standard in self-stabilization [<a href="#loc-44" role="doc-biblioref">Alt+19</a>, <a href="#loc-57" role="doc-biblioref">Dij74</a>, <a href="#loc-59" role="doc-biblioref">Dol00</a>], and self-stabilizing <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>-coloring under a central daemon goes back to [<a href="#loc-80" role="doc-biblioref">GT00</a>, <a href="#loc-84" role="doc-biblioref">HJS03</a>]. Up to its palette, the rule below is the second algorithm of [<a href="#loc-84" role="doc-biblioref">HJS03</a>].</p><p><strong>Network.</strong> The network is an undirected graph <math><mi>𝐺</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑉</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐸</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> with <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝑉</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></math> vertices. Two vertices <math><mi>𝑢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></math> are <em>neighbors</em> if <math><mi>𝑢</mi><mi>𝑣</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝐸</mi></math>. The neighborhood of <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> is <math><mi>𝒩︀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑢</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, its degree <math><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝒩︀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑢</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></math>, and <math><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">max</mo><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub></math> is the maximum degree. Each vertex hosts a process, and we identify the two.</p><p><strong>State, guard, action.</strong> Each process holds a <em>color</em> drawn from a palette of size <math><mi>𝑞</mi></math>. We consider the classical self-stabilizing coloring rule with the <em>conflict</em> (or <em>clash</em>) guard: a process is <em>enabled</em> iff it shares its color with at least one neighbor. When activated, an enabled process recolors itself with any color absent from its neighborhood. We take the palette large enough that a free color always exists, <math><mi>𝑞</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, so an enabled process always has a color to move to. A configuration is <em>legitimate</em> iff no process is enabled, that is, iff the coloring is proper.</p><p><strong>Daemon.</strong> We use the <em>central</em> (sequential) daemon, under which exactly one enabled process executes its action at each step, in its <em>random</em> version: the process is drawn uniformly at random among the enabled ones. The stabilization time <math><mi>𝑇</mi></math> is the number of activations, which is also the number of steps, until the configuration is legitimate. We write <math><msub><mi>𝑇</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> when the dependence on <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> matters. By <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a> below, <math><mi>𝑇</mi></math> does not depend on which free color a process picks. The random central daemon is our model, but two scheduler-free settings give the same number of recolorings in law (<a href="#prop-scheduler-free">Proposition 1</a>): a daemon that draws at each step a process uniformly among all <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math>, enabled or not, and a network in which every process wakes up at the ticks of its own Poisson clock of rate <math><mn>1</mn></math> and moves if it is enabled, reading its neighbors and writing its color in one atomic step (composite atomicity).</p><p><strong>Rounds.</strong> Rounds carry no information here: the set of enabled processes only shrinks along an execution (<a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a>), so every execution from a non-legitimate configuration takes exactly one round (a round ends once every process enabled at its start has moved or ceased to be enabled), under any central daemon.</p><p><strong>Initial configuration and colors.</strong> The algorithm may start from any configuration. Two reference distributions give explicit averaged formulas: the <em>monochrome</em> configuration, where all processes start with the same color, and the <em>random</em> configuration, where each process starts with an independent uniform color among <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> colors (not necessarily a proper coloring). Here <math><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑞</mi></math>, and <math><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> is the monochrome case. The palette size <math><mi>𝑞</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> guarantees a free color and nothing else, so <math><mi>𝑇</mi></math> depends on <math><mi>𝑞</mi></math> only through this inequality, while <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> enters our formulas through the probability <math><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math> that a given edge is initially in conflict.<sup id="loc-23" role="doc-noteref"><a href="#loc-109">1</a></sup></p><p><strong>Variants.</strong> The choice of guard matters, the choice of action does not. Under the Grundy-type guard, where a process is enabled as soon as its color is not the smallest one absent from its neighborhood, a process may move several times and our analysis does not apply. Under the other daemons the law of <math><mi>𝑇</mi></math> is not covered: the order of the moves is no longer uniform (locally central), or neighbors may move together (synchronous, distributed). <a href="#sec-conclusion">Section 6</a> discusses these cases.</p></div>
```

{#sec-general}
## 3 General theorems for the mean and the variance

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><p>Throughout, the vertices carry an initial coloring (fixed, monochrome, or i.i.d. uniform among <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> colors) and a uniform random labeling by distinct integers, which the next lemma links to the daemon. Equivalently, the labels are i.i.d. uniform on <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>, since only their relative order matters, and the proofs use this version. A vertex <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> is a <em>peak</em> if its label is larger than the label of every neighbor sharing its color (in the ordering of the introduction, a large label is a late turn). A vertex with no same-colored neighbor is a peak. The number of peaks is written <math><mi>𝑆</mi></math>, <math><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math>, <math><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜎</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> or <math><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐻</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> according to what is fixed (the size, the labeling, the graph).</p></div>
```

{#the-reduction-lemma}
### 3.1 The reduction lemma

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><div class="env env-lemma" id="lem-reduction"><div><strong>Lemma 1 (Reduction).</strong><div class="em"><p>Fix an initial coloring, a palette <math><mi>𝑞</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and a free-color recoloring policy that depends only on the current configuration and on internal coins independent of the labeling. Let <math><mi>𝜎</mi></math> be a labeling of <math><mi>𝑉</mi></math> by distinct integers and consider the <em>smallest-label schedule</em>, which at each step activates the enabled vertex of smallest label.</p><ol><li>Each vertex is activated at most once, and a vertex that is not enabled never becomes enabled.</li><li>A vertex is activated if and only if it is not a peak of the initial coloring under <math><mi>𝜎</mi></math>. The schedule therefore performs <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜎</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> moves, <math><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜎</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> being the number of peaks.</li><li>If <math><mi>𝜎</mi></math> is a uniform random labeling, the smallest-label schedule has the law of the random central daemon, so that <math><msub><mi>𝑇</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> in law, <math><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> being the number of peaks of a uniform random labeling.</li></ol></div></div></div><div><p><em>Proof.</em> (1) A move recolors its process with a color absent from the neighborhood, so it never creates a conflict: a process that has moved has no conflict and never regains one, and a process without conflict never acquires one. Writing <math><msub><mi>𝐴</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math> for the set of processes activated before step <math><mi>𝑡</mi></math> and <math><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math> for the set of enabled ones, <math><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math> consists of the processes outside <math><msub><mi>𝐴</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math> that have a same-colored neighbor outside <math><msub><mi>𝐴</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math>, and <math><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mrow><mi>𝑡</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>⊆</mo><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub><mo>∖</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝑢</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>, where <math><msub><mi>𝑢</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math> is the process activated at step <math><mi>𝑡</mi></math>.</p><p>(2) If <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> is a peak, every same-colored neighbor <math><mi>𝑤</mi></math> of <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> has a smaller label and, as long as <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> holds its initial color, is enabled until it acts. Under the smallest-label schedule <math><mi>𝑤</mi></math> acts before <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> and recolors away from <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math>’s color, so once all of them have acted <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> has no conflict and is never activated. If <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> is not a peak, it has a same-colored neighbor <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> of larger label. The two stay in conflict until one of them acts, <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> cannot act first, and the schedule stops after at most <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> moves by (1), so <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> acts.</p><p>(3) The history of the schedule before step <math><mi>𝑡</mi></math>, that is, the activated processes and the colors they chose, determines <math><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math>. Given the policy’s coins, independent of <math><mi>𝜎</mi></math>, this history is the event that <math><mi>𝜎</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑢</mi><mi>𝑠</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>𝜎</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑥</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for all <math><mi>𝑥</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑠</mi></msub><mo>∖</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝑢</mi><mi>𝑠</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and all <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math>. Since <math><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub><mo>⊆</mo><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑠</mi></msub><mo>∖</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝑢</mi><mi>𝑠</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> for every <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math> by (1), permuting the labels of <math><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math> among themselves leaves this event unchanged. Conditionally on the history, the relative order of the labels of <math><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math> is therefore uniform, and the process of smallest label in <math><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math>, the one the schedule activates, is uniform on <math><msub><mi>𝐸</mi><mi>𝑡</mi></msub></math>. This is one step of the random central daemon, and the two executions have the same law by induction on <math><mi>𝑡</mi></math>. <math><mi>∎</mi></math></p></div><p>The policy entered the proof only through “picks a free color”, and the daemon only through the uniform order of first activations, which two scheduler-free models share.</p><div class="env env-proposition" id="prop-scheduler-free"><div><strong>Proposition 1 (Scheduler-free readings).</strong> <em>The number of moves has the law <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> of <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a> in each of the two following models. (1) At each step a process is drawn uniformly among all <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> processes and moves if it is enabled, doing nothing otherwise. The number of steps until legitimacy is then the time needed to draw <math><mi>𝐽</mi></math> distinct processes, <math><mi>𝐽</mi></math> being the rank of the last non-peak in the order of first draws (<math><mi>𝐽</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> if the initial configuration is legitimate). Its mean given <math><mi>𝐽</mi></math> is <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐻</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐻</mi><mrow><mi>𝑛</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mi>𝐽</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, with <math><msub><mi>𝐻</mi><mi>𝑚</mi></msub></math> the <math><mi>𝑚</mi></math>-th harmonic number, and since <math><mi>𝐽</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math> the mean number of steps is at most <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐻</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, with equality on the monochrome clique. (2) Every process carries an independent Poisson clock of rate <math><mn>1</mn></math> and moves at each of its ticks at which it is enabled. The time until legitimacy is the first tick of the last non-peak, in the order of first ticks.</em></div></div><p>The proof (<a href="#sec-app-general">Appendix A</a>) labels every process by the rank of its first draw or first tick, a uniform random permutation, and observes that a process moves at its first activation iff it is not a peak, and never again.</p><div class="env env-proposition" id="prop-fixed-config"><div><strong>Proposition 2 (Fixed initial configuration).</strong><div class="em"><p>Let <math><mi>𝛾</mi></math> be an initial configuration and <math><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub></math> its <em>conflict graph</em>, the spanning subgraph of <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> whose edges join two vertices with the same color under <math><mi>𝛾</mi></math>, and let <math><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐻</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be the number of local maxima of a labeling on <math><mi>𝐻</mi></math>, <math><mi>𝛼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐻</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> its independence number and <math><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐻</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> its number of connected components.</p><ol><li><math><mi>𝑇</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> in law: every monochrome result of this paper applies to <math><mi>𝛾</mi></math> once <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> is replaced by <math><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub></math>, and in particular <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mi>𝑇</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> with <math><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> the number of neighbors of <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> sharing its color (<a href="#thm-mean">Theorem 1</a> below).</li><li><math><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for every labeling, so under a common labeling the monochrome configuration stabilizes last: it has the largest <math><mtext>ℙ</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for every <math><mi>𝑡</mi></math>.</li><li>Over all central and locally central daemons (the latter activate at each step a set of pairwise non-adjacent enabled processes), random or not, the number of moves from <math><mi>𝛾</mi></math> takes exactly the values <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝛼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. The worst case over configurations and schedules is <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.</li></ol></div></div></div><p>Parts (1) and (2) are <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a> read on <math><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub></math> and the fact that a local maximum of <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> is one of its spanning subgraph <math><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub></math>. The comparison in (2) is in law, not in variance: on <math><msub><mi>𝐾</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math>, recoloring one vertex of the smaller side raises the variance from <math><mn>9</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>20</mn></math> to <math><mn>11</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>16</mn></math>. For (3), labeling the processes of any execution in activation order makes it a smallest-label schedule by <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a>(1). A step of a locally central daemon can be serialized without changing the moves, and the sets of local maxima of labelings are exactly the independent sets that meet every component (<a href="#sec-app-general">Appendix A</a>).</p><p>With <math><mi>𝑚</mi></math> the number of initially conflicting processes, the worst case reads <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑚</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>𝜅</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, <math><msup><mi>𝜅</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math> counting the components of <math><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub></math> that have an edge. The folklore bound of <math><mi>𝑚</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math> moves (in each conflict component at least one process never moves) is thus tight exactly when there is one such component. The best schedule needs <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝛼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> moves (NP-hard to compute) and the worst <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> (linear time). By part (1) the random daemon exceeds the best schedule on average by exactly <math><mi>𝛼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, the slack of the Caro-Wei bound.</p><p>The peaks of a monochrome labeling are also a known object elsewhere: the vertices selected in the first round of the random-priority algorithm for maximal independent set <span id="loc-24">[</span><a href="#loc-42" role="doc-biblioref">ABI86</a>, <a href="#loc-90" role="doc-biblioref">Lub86</a>, <a href="#loc-92" role="doc-biblioref">Mét+11</a>]. The same random order drives the greedy algorithms whose parallel depth is studied by <span id="loc-25">[</span><a href="#loc-48" role="doc-biblioref">BFS12</a>] and <span id="loc-26">[</span><a href="#loc-74" role="doc-biblioref">FN20</a>], where every vertex eventually acts and the depth is the quantity of interest, whereas here the quantity is the number of moves.</p></div>
```

{#the-mean}
### 3.2 The mean

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><div class="env env-theorem" id="thm-mean"><div><strong>Theorem 1 (Mean).</strong><div class="em"><p>Let <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> be a graph on <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> vertices, possibly random, and let <math><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>𝑑</mi></msub></math> be the probability that a uniformly random vertex has degree <math><mi>𝑑</mi></math> (averaged over <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> when <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> is random). Give every vertex an independent uniform color among <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>. The expected number of peaks is</p><div class="eq" id="eq-mean-peaks"><math display="block"><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>𝑘</mi><munder><mo form="prefix">∑</mo><mi>𝑑</mi></munder><mfrac><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>𝑑</mi></msub><mrow><mi>𝑑</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>𝑘</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>𝑑</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">,</mo></math><div class="eq-num">(1)</div></div>and hence the mean stabilization time is <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑇</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. For <math><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> this gives the monochrome case <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑇</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><msub><mo form="prefix">∑</mo><mi>𝑑</mi></msub><mfrac><mi>𝑑</mi><mrow><mi>𝑑</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>𝑑</mi></msub></math>.</div></div></div><p>The proof (<a href="#sec-app-general">Appendix A</a>) conditions on the degree <math><mi>𝑑</mi></math> of a uniform vertex and on its number <math><mi>𝑚</mi><mo>∼</mo><mtext>Binomial</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑑</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> of same-colored neighbors, which it beats with probability <math><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑚</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>𝑡</mi><mi>𝑚</mi></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math>. The mean depends on the graph <em>only</em> through its degree distribution <math><mi>𝒑</mi></math>. The factor <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>𝑘</mi></mfrac></math> is the probability that a given edge is initially in conflict: for the mean, a <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-coloring on <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> behaves like the monochrome case on the random subgraph where each edge is kept with probability <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>𝑘</mi></mfrac></math> (on a forest the kept edges are independent and the equality holds in law, see <a href="#sec-trees">Section 5.2</a>). We write <math><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑑</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><msubsup><mo form="prefix">∫</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>𝑢</mi><mi>𝑑</mi></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>𝑢</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑑</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>𝑑</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for the peak probability of a degree-<math><mi>𝑑</mi></math> vertex, so that <math><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑑</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑑</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.</p></div>
```

{#the-variance}
### 3.3 The variance

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><p>By <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a>, <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑇</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, so the variance follows from the <em>second factorial moment</em> <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>𝑢</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">≠</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>ℙ</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mtext>both peaks</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Whether two vertices are both peaks depends on how their neighborhoods overlap, so the variance, unlike the mean, sees more of the graph than degrees. For an ordered pair of distinct vertices <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, let <math><mi>𝑎</mi></math> be the number of neighbors of <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> that are neither <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> nor a neighbor of <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math>, <math><mi>𝑐</mi></math> the symmetric count for <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math>, and <math><mi>𝑏</mi></math> the number of common neighbors. In the monochrome case only non-adjacent pairs contribute, since two adjacent vertices of the same color are never both peaks.</p><div class="env env-theorem" id="thm-sfm-mono"><div><strong>Theorem 2 (Second factorial moment, monochrome).</strong><div class="em"><p>In the monochrome case, the two vertices of an ordered non-adjacent pair with parameters <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are both peaks with probability</p><div class="eq"><math display="block"><mi>𝐽</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">,</mo></math><div class="eq-num">(2)</div></div><p>and those of an adjacent pair never are. With <math><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></msub></math> the probability that a random ordered pair is non-adjacent with parameters <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>,</p><div class="eq" id="eq-sfm-mono"><math display="block"><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><munder><mo form="prefix">∑</mo><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></munder><mfrac><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>.</mi></math><div class="eq-num">(3)</div></div></div></div></div><p>The proof (<a href="#sec-app-general">Appendix A</a>) conditions on the uniform labels <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math> of <math><mi>𝑢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></math>: a private neighbor of <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> ranks below <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> with probability <math><mi>𝑠</mi></math>, a common neighbor below both with probability <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">min</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and <math><mi>𝐽</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the integral of <math><msup><mi>𝑠</mi><mi>𝑎</mi></msup><msup><mi>𝑡</mi><mi>𝑐</mi></msup><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">min</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>𝑏</mi></msup></math> over the unit square. With <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> colors the same computation applies to <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑥</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math>, the probability that a given neighbor of a vertex of label <math><mi>𝑥</mi></math> fails to beat it (wrong color, or same color and lower label). Then <math><mi>𝑠</mi></math> is uniform on <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>. A common neighbor beats neither of two same-colored vertices with probability <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">min</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and neither of two differently colored ones with probability <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>.</p><div class="env env-theorem" id="thm-sfm"><div><strong>Theorem 3 (Second factorial moment).</strong><div class="em"><p>With every vertex colored uniformly among <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> colors, the two vertices of an ordered pair <math><mi>𝑢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></math> with parameters <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are both peaks with probability <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>same</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>dist</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> if non-adjacent and <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>dist</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> if adjacent, where <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>same</mtext></msub></math> (resp. <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>dist</mtext></msub></math>) is the probability that <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> and <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> are both peaks and received the same color (resp. distinct colors):</p><div class="eq" id="eq-tsame-tdist"><math display="block"><mtable class="multiline-equation aligned"><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>same</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><msubsup><mo form="prefix">∫</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup><msubsup><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∫</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>𝑠</mi><mi>𝑎</mi></msup><msup><mi>𝑡</mi><mi>𝑐</mi></msup><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">min</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>𝑏</mi></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>dist</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd><mo form="infix">=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>𝑘</mi><msubsup><mo form="prefix">∫</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup><msubsup><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∫</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>𝑠</mi><mi>𝑎</mi></msup><msup><mi>𝑡</mi><mi>𝑐</mi></msup><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>𝑏</mi></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mi>.</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></math><div class="eq-num">(4)</div></div><p>Then, with <math><msub><mi>𝑞</mi><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></msub></math> the probability that a random ordered pair is adjacent with parameters <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>,</p><div class="eq" id="eq-sfm"><math display="block"><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><munder><mo form="prefix">∑</mo><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>same</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>dist</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝑞</mi><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>dist</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>.</mi></math><div class="eq-num">(5)</div></div>At <math><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> one has <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>dist</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>same</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐽</mi></math>, recovering <a href="#thm-sfm-mono">Theorem 2</a>. Both integrals are elementary, and their values as finite sums are given in <a href="#sec-app-general">Appendix A</a>, where the theorem is proved.</div></div></div><div class="env env-corollary" id="cor-triangle-free"><div><strong>Corollary 1 (Pairs without common neighbor).</strong> <em>At <math><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> both integrands factorize, with <math><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><msubsup><mo form="prefix">∫</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>𝑠</mi><mi>𝑎</mi></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>𝑠</mi></math> as in <a href="#thm-mean">Theorem 1</a>: <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>same</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math> and <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>dist</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math>. Two non-adjacent vertices without common neighbor are thus independent peaks, for every <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>, and the covariance of two peak indicators vanishes beyond distance two. If <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> is triangle-free, adjacent pairs have <math><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and contribute <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math> each.</em></div></div><p>The variance is therefore a sum over the pairs at distance at most two,</p><div class="eq" id="eq-var-local"><math display="block"><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></munder><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><munder><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>𝑢</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">≠</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>dist</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑢</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">≤</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext>ℙ</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mtext>both peaks</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">,</mo></math><div class="eq-num">(6)</div></div><p>and it sees the profile <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> of these pairs, in particular the triangle count, and nothing else: the cycle <math><msub><mi>𝐶</mi><mn>6</mn></msub></math> and two disjoint triangles, both <math><mn>2</mn></math>-regular, have the same mean <math><mn>4</mn></math> and variances <math><mn>12</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>45</mn></math> and <math><mn>0</mn></math>. The maximum degree nevertheless bounds the fluctuations.</p><div class="env env-corollary" id="cor-concentration"><div><strong>Corollary 2 (Concentration and normal approximation).</strong><div class="em"><p>Let <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> have maximum degree <math><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></math>, with a fixed initial configuration or a uniform random <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-coloring.</p><ol><li>For every <math><mi>𝑡</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, <math><mtext>ℙ</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo>−</mo><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mi>𝑇</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mo>≥</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>2</mn><mo form="prefix" lspace="0.16666666666666666em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">exp</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix">−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>𝑡</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.</li><li>The Kolmogorov distance (the supremum distance between distribution functions) between the law of <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo>−</mo><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msqrt></math> and the standard normal law is at most <math><mi>𝐶</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>/</mi><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math> for an absolute constant <math><mi>𝐶</mi></math>. Along a sequence of graphs of bounded degree, <math><msub><mi>𝑇</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> is therefore asymptotically normal whenever <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑇</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>∞</mi></math>, in particular when <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑇</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is of order <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math>.</li></ol></div></div></div><p>The proof (<a href="#sec-app-general">Appendix A</a>) is the bounded differences inequality <span id="loc-27">[</span><a href="#loc-91" role="doc-biblioref">McD89</a>], the rank and color of a vertex influencing at most <math><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> peak indicators, and the normal approximation theorem for sums of variables with a dependency graph (a graph on the summands in which families with no edge between them are independent) <span id="loc-28">[</span><a href="#loc-50" role="doc-biblioref">BR89</a>, <a href="#loc-98" role="doc-biblioref">Rin94</a>], indicators at distance at least <math><mn>3</mn></math> depending on disjoint sets of variables. The number of local maxima of a random labeling is a standard example of this method <span id="loc-29">[</span><a href="#loc-51" role="doc-biblioref">BRS89</a>, <a href="#loc-79" role="doc-biblioref">Gol05</a>].</p></div>
```

{#sec-extremal}
## 4 Extremal graphs

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><p>Fix the number of vertices <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math>. We work in the monochrome regime (<math><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>), where a peak is a <em>local maximum</em>. By <a href="#prop-fixed-config">Proposition 2</a> the statements apply to any fixed configuration, once the graph is replaced by its conflict graph restricted to the initially conflicting processes and <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> by their number. The statements about the mean extend to every <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>, while those about the variance are specific to <math><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, a single edge having positive variance once <math><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. We use repeatedly that <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑆</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> (<a href="#thm-mean">Theorem 1</a>, the Caro-Wei bound) and that the peaks form an independent set containing the vertex of largest label, so <math><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑆</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝛼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Throughout, <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> is a <em>fixed</em> graph and the randomness is the labeling (randomized analogues in <a href="#sec-app-extremal">Appendix B</a>).</p></div>
```

{#extremes-of-the-mean}
### 4.1 Extremes of the mean

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><div class="env env-proposition" id="prop-mean-extremes"><div><strong>Proposition 3 (Mean extremes).</strong> <em>Among graphs on <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> vertices with no isolated vertex, <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is minimized by the perfect matching (for even <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math>, the graph of <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></math> disjoint edges, every vertex of degree <math><mn>1</mn></math>), at <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></math>, and maximized by the clique <math><msub><mi>𝐾</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math>, at <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Hence <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>. For odd <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> the minimum is <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mn>6</mn></math>, attained by a path on three vertices together with a perfect matching of the other vertices. The extremal graphs are the same for every <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>.</em></div></div><p>The proof (<a href="#sec-app-extremal">Appendix B</a>) is the termwise bound <math><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></math>, and the same for <math><msub><mi>𝜌</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub></math>, which is decreasing.</p></div>
```

{#zero-variance}
### 4.2 Zero variance

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><div class="env env-theorem" id="thm-zero-var"><div><strong>Theorem 4 (Zero variance).</strong> <em>In the monochrome case, <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> if and only if <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> is a disjoint union of cliques, in which case <math><mi>𝑇</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> deterministically, <math><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> being the number of connected components.</em></div></div><div><em>Proof.</em> If <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> is a disjoint union of cliques, every labeling of a clique has a unique local maximum, so <math><mi>𝑆</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> under any labeling. Conversely, a graph that is not such a union contains an induced path <math><mi>𝑎</mi><mi>𝑏</mi><mi>𝑐</mi></math>. Give <math><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></math> the three largest labels and fix the others. Every other vertex has the same peak status in all such labelings, while ranking <math><mi>𝑏</mi></math> below both <math><mi>𝑎</mi></math> and <math><mi>𝑐</mi></math> gives two peaks among <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and ranking it above both gives one, so <math><mi>𝑆</mi></math> is not constant. <math><mi>∎</mi></math></div></div>
```

{#maximal-variance-the-star}
### 4.3 Maximal variance: the star

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><p>At the other end the variance can be of order <math><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. On the star the stabilization time is essentially the rank of the center’s label, so it does not concentrate at all. To avoid clashing with the peak count <math><mi>𝑆</mi></math>, we write <math><msub><mtext>St</mtext><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> for the star on <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> vertices (one center, <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math> leaves), that is, the complete bipartite graph <math><msub><mi>𝐾</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>.</p><div class="env env-proposition" id="prop-star"><div><strong>Proposition 4 (Star law and variance).</strong><div class="em"><p>On the monochrome star <math><msub><mtext>St</mtext><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math>, <math><mtext>ℙ</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑗</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></math> for <math><mi>𝑗</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math><mtext>ℙ</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></math>. Hence</p><div class="eq" id="eq-star"><math display="block"><mtable class="multiline-equation aligned"><mtr><mtd><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd><mo form="infix">=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>𝑛</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo rspace="0em">,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd><mo form="infix">=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>𝑛</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mfrac><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>13</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑜</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>.</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></math><div class="eq-num">(7)</div></div></div></div></div><p>A leaf is a peak iff its label exceeds the center’s, so <math><mi>𝑇</mi></math> is the label rank of the center, except that the rank <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> also gives <math><mi>𝑇</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math> (<a href="#sec-app-extremal">Appendix B</a>). Since every leaf is compared with the same center, <math><mi>𝑆</mi></math> is almost uniform on <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. The matching upper bound for general graphs comes from a classification of the pairwise covariances, computed from <a href="#thm-sfm-mono">Theorem 2</a> (proof in <a href="#sec-app-extremal">Appendix B</a>).</p><div class="env env-lemma" id="lem-cov-bound"><div><strong>Lemma 2 (Pairwise covariance).</strong><div class="em"><p>Let <math><mi>𝑢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></math> be distinct vertices with peak indicators <math><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub></math>. If <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> and <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> are adjacent, <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Cov</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">−</mo><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. If they are non-adjacent with parameters <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then</p><div class="eq" id="eq-cov-closed"><math display="block"><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Cov</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>𝑏</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo rspace="0em">,</mo></math><div class="eq-num">(8)</div></div>that is <math><mi>𝑏</mi><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> divided by the number of vertices at distance at most one from <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> or from <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math>. Hence <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Cov</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> when <math><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>; <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Cov</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> when <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, which is <math><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn></math> at <math><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and at most <math><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>24</mn></math> otherwise; <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Cov</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>24</mn></math> when <math><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≠</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>; and <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Cov</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>18</mn></math> when <math><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. In particular <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Cov</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn></math> always, with equality exactly when <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> and <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> are two leaves hanging from the same vertex.</div></div></div><div class="env env-theorem" id="thm-var-upper"><div><strong>Theorem 5 (Variance upper bound).</strong> <em>For every graph on <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> vertices, monochrome, <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn></math>. Hence the maximum variance over <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math>-vertex graphs is <math><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑜</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, with sharp leading constant <math><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn></math>, attained to leading order by the star (<math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>13</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑜</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> on <math><msub><mtext>St</mtext><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> by <a href="#eq-star">Eq. (7)</a>).</em></div></div><div><em>Proof.</em> Write <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑆</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>𝑢</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">≠</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></mrow></msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Cov</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑢</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Each <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑋</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>4</mn></math>, so the first sum is at most <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>/</mi><mn>4</mn></math>.
```
