In the second, adjacent ordered pairs contribute negatively and, by <a href="#lem-cov-bound">Lemma 2</a>, each of the at most <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ordered pairs contributes at most <math><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn></math>, so the sum is at most <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn></math>. Adding, <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>/</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn></math>. The star’s variance <a href="#eq-star">Eq. (7)</a> has the same leading term <math><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><mn>12</mn></math>, so the constant is sharp. <math><mi>∎</mi></math></div><div class="env env-theorem" id="thm-star-exact"><div><strong>Theorem 6 (Exact variance maximizer).</strong> <em>For every <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, among all graphs on <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> vertices, <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is maximized by the star <math><msub><mtext>St</mtext><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> and by no other graph.</em></div></div><p>The proof (<a href="#sec-app-extremal">Appendix B</a>) sorts the vertices into leaves (degree one) and the others, bounds the variance through <a href="#lem-cov-bound">Lemma 2</a> in terms of the number of leaves and of the largest number of leaves at a single vertex, and compares the bound with the star: it falls short of the star’s variance for every <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>7</mn></math> unless the graph is the star itself, and exhaustive enumeration settles <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>6</mn></math>. Isolated vertices are peaks of every labeling, so a graph that has some is compared with a smaller star.</p></div>
```

{#sec-families}
## 5 Applications to graph families

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><p>The mean of each family comes from <a href="#thm-mean">Theorem 1</a> alone and the variance from <a href="#thm-sfm">Theorem 3</a> through the local formula <a href="#eq-var-local">Eq. (6)</a>, and only <math><mi>𝐺</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> has triangles, that is, adjacent pairs with common neighbors. On paths, cycles and random trees the variance grows linearly in <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> and, from a monochrome start, the law is asymptotically normal. In the two Erdős-Rényi models at fixed <math><mi>𝑝</mi></math>, the expected number of peaks stays bounded and the peak count converges in law without normalization. The companion code checks the formulas below numerically (<a href="#sec-app-numerics">Appendix G</a>).</p></div>
```

### 5.2 Random trees

its size (<a href="#prop-tree-gw">Proposition 11</a>).</p><p>The Cayley analysis extends to rooted labeled trees with an arbitrary offspring distribution, and the <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-colored law to a functional equation (<a href="#thm-gtree">Proposition 12</a> in <a href="#sec-app-trees">Appendix D</a>), which Lagrange inversion solves in the Cayley case.</p><div class="env env-theorem" id="thm-tree-klaw"><div><strong>Theorem 10 (Random tree, exact law under a <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-coloring).</strong><div class="em"><p>Under a uniform random <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-coloring of the uniform random rooted labeled tree on <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> vertices, with <math><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></math> and <math><mi>𝐹</mi></math> the monochrome generating function <a href="#eq-tree-peak-gf">Eq. (14)</a>,</p><div class="eq" id="eq-tree-klaw"><math display="block"><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝑣</mi><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>𝑘</mi><mrow><mi>𝑛</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mi>𝑧</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><msup><mi>𝑒</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>𝐹</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑧</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mi>.</mi></math><div class="eq-num">(19)</div></div></div></div></div><p>Each non-root vertex has its parent’s color with probability <math><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math>, independently of the others: the conflicting edges are a random subset of the tree edges, and the <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-colored peak count is in law the monochrome peak count of this random forest. The trees containing a given spanning forest with component sizes <math><msub><mi>𝑐</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑐</mi><mi>𝑚</mi></msub></math> number <math><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mi>𝑚</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi>𝑐</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>⋯</mi><msub><mi>𝑐</mi><mi>𝑚</mi></msub></math> <span id="loc-40">[</span><a href="#loc-93" role="doc-biblioref">Moo70</a>, <a href="#loc-96" role="doc-biblioref">Pit99</a>], and summing over the forests gives <math><msup><mi>𝑒</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>𝐹</mi></mrow></msup></math> (<a href="#sec-app-trees">Appendix D</a>).</p></div>
```

{#erdos-renyi-g-n-p}
### 5.3 Erdős-Rényi 𝐺(𝑛,𝑝)

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><p>In <math><mi>𝐺</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> <span id="loc-41">[</span><a href="#loc-86" role="doc-biblioref">JŁR00</a>] a uniform vertex has degree <math><mi>𝑑</mi><mo>∼</mo><mtext>Binomial</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. The peak count has an explicit generating function. List the vertices by decreasing label, let <math><msub><mi>ℎ</mi><mi>𝑗</mi></msub></math> be the number of vertices preceding the <math><mi>𝑗</mi></math>-th one that share its color, and attribute each edge to its endpoint of smaller label: the <math><mi>𝑗</mi></math>-th vertex is a peak iff none of its <math><msub><mi>ℎ</mi><mi>𝑗</mi></msub></math> edges to these vertices is present, and these edge sets are disjoint for distinct <math><mi>𝑗</mi></math>, so that, given the colors, the <math><mi>𝑗</mi></math>-th vertex is a peak independently of the others with probability <math><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>ℎ</mi><mi>𝑗</mi></msub></msup></math>. Marking peaks by <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math>, <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝑣</mi><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>𝔼</mtext><msubsup><mo form="prefix">∏</mo><mrow><mi>𝑗</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>𝑛</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>ℎ</mi><mi>𝑗</mi></msub></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Monochrome, <math><msub><mi>ℎ</mi><mi>𝑗</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑗</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, so <math><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> has probability generating function</p><div class="eq" id="eq-er-gf"><math display="block"><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mrow><mi>𝑛</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑝</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∏</mo><mrow><mi>𝑗</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>𝑛</mi></munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>𝑗</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>.</mi></math><div class="eq-num">(20)</div></div><p>With <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> colors, <math><msub><mi>ℎ</mi><mi>𝑗</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mtext>Binomial</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑗</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Conditioning instead on the color composition <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, which is multinomial, gives the product of the monochrome series of the color classes,</p><div class="eq" id="eq-er-gf-k"><math display="block"><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mrow><mi>𝑛</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑘</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mspace width="1em"></mspace><mspace width="1em"></mspace><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mi>𝑘</mi><mi>𝑝</mi></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>𝑛</mi></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>.</mi></math><div class="eq-num">(22)</div></div>Moreover the mean at <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> equals the mean at <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>: for the mean, though not for the variance, a random <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-coloring at edge probability <math><mi>𝑝</mi></math> behaves like the monochrome case at edge probability <math><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math>.</div></div></div><p>The mean is <math><msub><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mi>𝑗</mi></msub><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>𝑗</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>𝑛</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>𝑗</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>. The variance is in <a href="#sec-app-er">Appendix E</a> in two closed forms: a direct one, from the same reading of the series (<a href="#prop-er-sfm">Proposition 13</a>), and one that averages <a href="#thm-sfm">Theorem 3</a> over the multinomial neighborhood profile of a random pair (<a href="#prop-er-var">Proposition 14</a>), which the bipartite computation reuses. At fixed <math><mi>𝑝</mi></math> the expected number of peaks tends to <math><mi>𝑘</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑝</mi></math> and the variance tends to a constant, instead of growing linearly in <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math>.</p><div class="env env-proposition" id="prop-er-limit"><div><strong>Proposition 7 (Erdős-Rényi, limiting law).</strong><div class="em"><p>Monochrome, <math><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>𝑖</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>𝑛</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>𝐵</mi><mi>𝑖</mi></msub></math> with <math><msub><mi>𝐵</mi><mi>𝑖</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mtext>Bernoulli</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>𝑖</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> independent, <math><msub><mi>𝐵</mi><mi>𝑖</mi></msub></math> being the indicator that the vertex with exactly <math><mi>𝑖</mi></math> higher-labeled vertices is a peak. As <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>∞</mi></math>:</p><ol><li>For <em>fixed</em> <math><mi>𝑝</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, <math><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> converges in distribution to the non-degenerate integer-valued law of rspace="0em">≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>𝐵</mi><mi>𝑖</mi></msub></math>, with probability generating function <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝑣</mi><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>∞</mi></msub></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∏</mo><mrow><mi>𝑖</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>𝑖</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> random quantity that never becomes deterministic.</li><li>For <math><mi>𝑝</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></math> with <math><mi>𝑛</mi><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>∞</mi></math>, <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msqrt></math> converges to a standard normal law, with <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑝</mi></math> and <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.</li></ol><p>With <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> initial colors, <math><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>∞</mi></msub></math> is replaced by the sum of <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> independent copies of itself in the first regime, and in the second the normal limit persists, with <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑝</mi></math> and <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.</p></div></div></div><p>The proof (<a href="#sec-app-er">Appendix E</a>) reads the factorization of <a href="#eq-er-gf">Eq. (20)</a> as a sum of independent indicators, applies Borel-Cantelli at fixed <math><mi>𝑝</mi></math> and the central limit theorem for <math><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, and conditions on the color classes for <math><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></math>.</p></div>

lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><msub><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>.</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></math><div class="eq-num">(23)</div></div></div></div></div><p>The proofs are in <a href="#sec-app-bip">Appendix F</a>, with the variance, which follows from the same averaging over the multinomial neighborhood counts as for <math><mi>𝐺</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, split according to the sides of the pair (<a href="#prop-bip-var">Proposition 15</a>). The peak count again has a product structure, now conditional on how the two sides and the colors interleave in the label order.</p><div class="env env-proposition" id="prop-bip-limit"><div><strong>Proposition 9 (Bipartite Erdős-Rényi, generating function and limit law).</strong><div class="em"><p>List the vertices by decreasing label and let <math><msub><mi>ℎ</mi><mi>𝑗</mi></msub></math> be the number of vertices preceding the <math><mi>𝑗</mi></math>-th one that lie on the other side of the bipartition and share its color. Conditionally on the sequence of sides and colors, the <math><mi>𝑗</mi></math>-th vertex is a peak independently of the others with probability <math><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>ℎ</mi><mi>𝑗</mi></msub></msup></math>, so <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝑣</mi><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>𝔼</mtext><msubsup><mo form="prefix">∏</mo><mrow><mi>𝑗</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>𝑛</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>ℎ</mi><mi>𝑗</mi></msub></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, the outer expectation being over the uniform interleaving of <math><msub><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math><msub><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> sides and over the colors. If <math><mi>𝑝</mi></math> is fixed and <math><msub><mi>𝑛</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑛</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>𝜆</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then, monochrome, <math><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math> converges in distribution to an almost surely finite random variable <math><msubsup><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>∞</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></math>, with</p><div class="eq"><math display="block"><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>∞</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>𝜆</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝜆</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>𝑝</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝜆</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>𝜆</mi><mi>𝑝</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo rspace="0em">,</mo></math><div class="eq-num">(24)</div></div>and with <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> initial colors the limit is the sum of <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> independent copies of <math><msubsup><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>∞</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></math>.</div></div></div><p>In the regime <math><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></math> the law should again be Gaussian, but the interleaving contributes to the variance at the same order as the conditional fluctuations, and we leave this regime open.</p></div>
```

{#sec-conclusion}
## 6 Conclusion and future work

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><p>Everything here follows from <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a>, which holds for every initial configuration and makes the monochrome one the slowest for every labeling. We leave open the central limit theorem for the <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-colored tree, which the linear variance <a href="#eq-tree-kvar">Eq. (18)</a> and the <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math>-th power in <a href="#eq-tree-klaw">Eq. (19)</a> suggest, and the regime <math><mi>𝑝</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></math> of the bipartite model.</p><p>On the model side, the Grundy-type guard and the daemons beyond the central one change the dynamics. Under the locally central daemon the executions, once serialized, and the range of the number of moves are the same as under the central daemon (<a href="#prop-fixed-config">Proposition 2</a>), but a random locally central daemon no longer induces a uniform order, and its mean number of moves is open. Under the synchronous daemon and an adversarial distributed daemon the deterministic rule does not stabilize in anonymous networks, which is why the algorithms of [<a href="#loc-80" role="doc-biblioref">GT00</a>] and [<a href="#loc-47" role="doc-biblioref">Ber+10</a>] use identifiers or coins. Since it converges whenever the moves are serialized, it is weak-stabilizing, and under a randomized distributed daemon it stabilizes with probability one [<a href="#loc-62" role="doc-biblioref">DTY15</a>]. The law of its number of moves is then open. Finally, the reduction needs only that a process which has moved never moves again and never enables a neighbor. Under the Grundy-type guard a process may move several times, and what replaces the peak count for such rules is open.</p></div>
```

## A Proofs for Section 3

```{raw} html
<div class="typst"><div><strong>Proposition 1 (restated).</strong> <em>Under a daemon drawing uniformly among all processes, with null activations, and under independent Poisson clocks, the number of moves has the law <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></math>.</em></div><div><em>Proof of <a href="#prop-scheduler-free">Proposition 1</a>.</em> Label every process by the rank of its first draw, or of its first tick. This gives a uniform random permutation. At the first activation of a process <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math>, its same-colored neighbors of smaller label have been activated earlier, while <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> still held its initial color, hence in conflict, and have moved away from that color, while those of larger label still hold it. So <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> moves at its first activation iff it is not a peak, and never again by <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a>(1). The configuration becomes legitimate when the last non-peak is activated for the first time, since every initially conflicting edge has a non-peak endpoint and moves never create conflicts. In model (1) the gaps between successive first draws are independent of the order in which the processes first appear, so given that order the number of steps until the <math><mi>𝐽</mi></math>-th distinct process is drawn has mean <math><msubsup><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>𝑖</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>𝐽</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mi>𝑛</mi><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐻</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐻</mi><mrow><mi>𝑛</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mi>𝐽</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. The last process drawn carries the largest label and is always a peak, so <math><mi>𝐽</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, with <math><mi>𝐽</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math> on the monochrome clique, where every other process is a non-peak. <math><mi>∎</mi></math></div><div><strong>Proposition 2 (restated).</strong> <em>For an initial configuration <math><mi>𝛾</mi></math> with conflict graph <math><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub></math>: (1) <math><mi>𝑇</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> in law, hence <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mi>𝑇</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∑</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>; (2) <math><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for every labeling; (3) over all central and locally central daemons the number of moves takes exactly the values <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝛼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.</em></div><div><em>Proof of <a href="#prop-fixed-config">Proposition 2</a>.</em> (1) Under <math><mi>𝛾</mi></math> two neighbors are in conflict exactly when they are adjacent in <math><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub></math>, and a peak is a local maximum of <math><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub></math>, so this is <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a> with the definition unfolded, and the mean follows from <math><mtext>ℙ</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mtext>is a peak</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑑</mi><mi>𝑣</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. (2) A vertex whose label exceeds those of its neighbors in <math><mi>𝐺</mi></math> exceeds those of its neighbors in the subgraph <math><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub></math>. (3) Every execution under a central daemon is the smallest-label schedule of some labeling: label the processes activated in the execution <math><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑇</mi></math> in activation order and the others arbitrarily above <math><mi>𝑇</mi></math>. By <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a>(1) an activated process is never enabled again, so at step <math><mi>𝑡</mi></math> the enabled process of smallest label is the one labeled <math><mi>𝑡</mi></math>, and the execution has <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> moves for that labeling. A step of a locally central daemon activates pairwise non-adjacent processes and can be serialized in any order without changing the moves, so the same holds for these daemons. Conversely every labeling yields an execution. Local maxima form an independent set meeting every component (each component contains its largest label), so <math><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑆</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝛼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and every independent set <math><mi>𝐼</mi></math> meeting every component is the set of local maxima of some labeling: give the largest labels to <math><mi>𝐼</mi></math> and let the other labels decrease with the distance to <math><mi>𝐼</mi></math>. Removing vertices one at a time from a maximum independent set, inside the components where it has at least two, gives such sets of every size between <math><mi>𝛼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Finally <math><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐺</mi><mi>𝛾</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>𝜅</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐺</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, with equality for the monochrome configuration. <math><mi>∎</mi></math></div><div><strong>Theorem 1 (restated).</strong> <em>Under a uniform <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-coloring the expected number of peaks is given by <a href="#eq-mean-peaks">Eq. (1)</a>.</em></div><div><p><em>Proof of <a href="#thm-mean">Theorem 1</a>.</em> By linearity, <math><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo lspace="0.2222222222222222em" rspace="0.2222222222222222em">⋅</mo><mtext>ℙ</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mtext>is a peak</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for a uniformly random vertex <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math>. Condition on the degree of <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> being <math><mi>𝑑</mi></math>. The <math><mi>𝑑</mi></math> neighbors of <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> each share <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math>’s color independently with probability <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>𝑘</mi></mfrac></math>, so the number <math><mi>𝑚</mi></math> of same-colored neighbors is <math><mtext>Binomial</mtext><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>𝑑</mi><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>𝑘</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>. Given <math><mi>𝑚</mi></math>, the labels of <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> and these <math><mi>𝑚</mi></math> neighbors are in uniform random relative order, so <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> is the maximum with probability <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑚</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>𝑡</mi><mi>𝑚</mi></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math>. lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>.</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></math><div class="eq-num">(25)</div></div>Averaging over <math><mi>𝑑</mi></math> with weights <math><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mi>𝑑</mi></msub></math> and multiplying by <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> gives <a href="#eq-mean-peaks">Eq. (1)</a>. <math><mi>∎</mi></math></div><div><strong>Theorem 2 (restated).</strong><div class="em"><p>In the monochrome case, the two vertices of an ordered non-adjacent pair with parameters <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are both peaks with probability</p><math display="block"><mi>𝐽</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">,</mo></math><p>and those of an adjacent pair never are. With <math><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></msub></math> the probability that a random ordered pair is non-adjacent with parameters <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>,</p><math display="block"><mtext>𝔼</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑆</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><munder><mo form="prefix">∑</mo><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></munder><mfrac><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>.</mi></math></div></div><div><em>Proof of <a href="#thm-sfm-mono">Theorem 2</a>.</em> Assign i.i.d. uniform <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math> ranks. Since the peak condition depends only on relative order, these have the same law as a uniform random labeling. Condition on the ranks <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math> of <math><mi>𝑢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi></math>: each of the <math><mi>𝑎</mi></math> private neighbors of <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> must rank below <math><mi>𝑠</mi></math>, each of the <math><mi>𝑐</mi></math> private neighbors of <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> below <math><mi>𝑡</mi></math>, and each of the <math><mi>𝑏</mi></math> common neighbors below <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">min</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, so <math><mtext>ℙ</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑣</mi><mspace width="0.2222em"></mspace><mtext>both peaks</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><msubsup><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em">∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>𝑠</mi><mi>𝑎</mi></msup><msup><mi>𝑡</mi><mi>𝑐</mi></msup><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">min</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>𝑏</mi></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math>, and splitting on <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math> and <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math> evaluates this to <math><mi>𝐽</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Summing over pairs with weights <math><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></msub></math> and using <a href="#lem-reduction">Lemma 1</a> gives <a href="#eq-sfm-mono">Eq. (3)</a>. <math><mi>∎</mi></math></div><div><strong>Theorem 3 (restated).</strong> <em>The joint peak probabilities of a pair with parameters <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑎</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> under a uniform <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math>-coloring are the double integrals <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>same</mtext></msub></math> and <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>dist</mtext></msub></math> of <a href="#eq-tsame-tdist">Eq. (4)</a>, and the second factorial moment is given by <a href="#eq-sfm">Eq. (5)</a>.</em></div><div><p><em>Proof of <a href="#thm-sfm">Theorem 3</a>.</em> Realize the labeling by i.i.d. uniform ranks and condition on the ranks <math><mi>𝑥</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑦</mi></math> and on the colors of <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> and <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math>. A neighbor of <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> prevents <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> from being a peak iff it has the color of <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> and a rank above <math><mi>𝑥</mi></math>, an event of probability <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑥</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math>, independently across neighbors, so each private neighbor of <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> leaves <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> a peak with probability <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑥</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math>, and each private neighbor of <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> leaves <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> a peak with probability <math><mi>𝑡</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑦</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math>. A common neighbor leaves both <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> and <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> peaks with probability <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">min</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> when <math><mi>𝑢</mi></math> and <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> share a color (it needs another color, or a rank below both) and <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math> when they do not (it must avoid two disjoint events of probabilities <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑥</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math> and <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑦</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math>). Given the colors and the ranks, both are therefore peaks with probability <math><msup><mi>𝑠</mi><mi>𝑎</mi></msup><msup><mi>𝑡</mi><mi>𝑐</mi></msup><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">min</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>𝑏</mi></msup></math> in the first case and <math><msup><mi>𝑠</mi><mi>𝑎</mi></msup><msup><mi>𝑡</mi><mi>𝑐</mi></msup><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>𝑏</mi></msup></math> in the second. As <math><mi>𝑥</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑦</mi></math> are uniform on <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>, the variables <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math> are uniform on <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math> with density <math><mi>𝑘</mi></math> each, and the two cases have probabilities <math><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math> and <math><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math>: this is <a href="#eq-tsame-tdist">Eq. (4)</a>. Two adjacent vertices of the same color are never both peaks, and adjacency does not enter the second case, so adjacent pairs contribute <math><msub><mi>𝜋</mi><mtext>dist</mtext></msub></math> only. Summing over ordered pairs with the weights <math><msub><mi>𝑝</mi><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></msub></math> and <math><msub><mi>𝑞</mi><mrow><mi>𝑎</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑏</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mi>𝑐</mi></mrow></msub></math> gives <a href="#eq-sfm">Eq. (5)</a>. In the original variables, with <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑥</mi><mi>𝑦</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑡</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑘</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>𝑦</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mi>𝑘</mi></math> parametrizing the half of the square where <math><mi>𝑠</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑡</mi></math> (Jacobian The peak count is a function of these <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> independent variables, and changing one of them changes the peak status of <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> and of its neighbors only, hence by at most <math><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, so (1) is the bounded differences inequality [<a href="#loc-91" role="doc-biblioref">McD89</a>]. For (2), the indicator that <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> is a peak depends only on the variables of <math><mi>𝑣</mi></math> and its neighbors, so two families of indicators whose vertices are pairwise at distance at least <math><mn>3</mn></math> depend on disjoint sets of independent variables and are independent. The graph joining pairs at distance at most <math><mn>2</mn></math>, of maximum degree at most <math><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, is thus a dependency graph for the indicators, and the normal approximation theorem for sums of bounded variables with a dependency graph [<a href="#loc-50" role="doc-biblioref">BR89</a>, <a href="#loc-98" role="doc-biblioref">Rin94</a>] bounds the Kolmogorov distance by a constant times <math><mi>𝑛</mi><msup><mi>𝐷</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><msup><mi>𝜎</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mi>𝑛</mi></msqrt><msup><mi>𝐷</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>/</mi><msup><mi>𝜎</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐷</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>𝜎</mi></math> with <math><mi>𝐷</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> (one plus the maximum degree of the dependency graph) and <math><msup><mi>𝜎</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑇</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Since <math><msup><mi>𝜎</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mi>𝑛</mi><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></math> by the Efron-Stein inequality applied to the same <math><mi>𝑛</mi></math> variables, and <math><msup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>𝐷</mi></math>, the first term dominates the other two, and <math><msup><mi>𝐷</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></math>. The bound tends to <math><mn>0</mn></math> exactly when <math><msup><mi>𝜎</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><msup><mi>𝑛</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>∞</mi></math>. For a slower growth of the variance it says nothing, and we do not claim normality there. <math><mi>∎</mi></math></div><p>On the path the second factorial moment reproduces <math><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.16666666666666666em">Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑇</mi><msub><mi>𝑃</mi><mi>𝑛</mi></msub></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mn>45</mn></math> for <math><mi>𝑛</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>4</mn></math>.</p></div>
